summary: A rich young ruler asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, but goes away sorrowful when Jesus tells him to sell everything and follow Him.
key_insight: Jesus lists only the commandments about neighbors, and the man says he has kept them all. Then one command, sell and follow Me, tests the commandments Jesus left unspoken: whether God comes first, and whether he covets. Mark says Jesus loved him as He said it.
story: As Jesus set out on the road, a man came running and knelt before Him. {Mk} He was young {Mt} and a ruler. {Lk} “Good Teacher,” he asked, “what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” {Mk}

“Why do you call Me good?” Jesus said. “No one is good but One, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.” “Which ones?” the man asked. {Mt} Jesus named them: “Do not commit adultery,” “Do not murder,” “Do not steal,” “Do not bear false witness,” “Do not defraud,” “Honor your father and your mother.” {Mk} Matthew adds, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” {Mt}
“Teacher, all these things I have kept from my youth,” {Mk} he said. “What do I still lack?” {Mt}

Then Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said, “One thing you lack: Go your way, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, take up the cross, and follow Me.” {Mk} When he heard this, he became very sorrowful, for he was very rich, {Lk} and he went away.

Jesus looked around at His disciples. “How hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God!” The disciples were astonished, and He said again, “Children, how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” {Mk}
Greatly astonished, they asked, “Who then can be saved?” Jesus looked at them and said, “With men it is impossible, but not with God; for with God all things are possible.” {Mk}

Peter said, “See, we have left all and followed You. Therefore what shall we have?” {Mt} Jesus promised that when the Son of Man sits on the throne of His glory, the Twelve would sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. {Mt} Everyone who has left home or family or lands for His sake and the gospel’s will receive a hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and in the age to come, eternal life. {Mk} “But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
differences: Matthew calls him a young man and Luke a ruler; Mark says he came running and knelt.
Matthew records the man asking “Which ones?” and adds “love your neighbor as yourself” to the list; Mark alone has “Do not defraud.”
Only Mark says Jesus looked at him and “loved him,” and only Mark adds “take up the cross.”
Only Matthew records the promise of twelve thrones; only Mark adds “with persecutions.”
In the NKJV all three record “Why do you call Me good?” Many modern translations, following older manuscripts of Matthew, word Matthew’s account differently.

fit.question: In the NKJV, Matthew agrees with Mark and Luke: the man says “Good Teacher,” and Jesus asks, “Why do you call Me good?” But many modern translations follow older manuscripts of Matthew, where the man says only Teacher and Jesus asks why he is asking Him about what is good. Did Jesus question the title or the question?

points.label: Two families of manuscripts
points.text: The NKJV follows the majority of Greek manuscripts, in which all three Gospels match. Some of the oldest manuscripts of Matthew have the other wording. Faithful scholars differ on which reading Matthew wrote; the words in Mark and Luke are not in doubt.

points.label: Good twice
points.text: The man used the word good twice: he called Jesus good, and he asked what good thing he should do (Matthew 19:16). Jesus’ reply answers both, because only God is truly good. Mark and Luke record the part about the title; the older text of Matthew records the part about the deed.

points.label: The same point
points.text: In every version Jesus says that only One is good, and that One is God. Each account turns the man away from his own goodness toward God.

fit.note: Whichever wording Matthew wrote, each Gospel gives a true part of one conversation, and the point is the same: only God is good.
fit.short: The man spoke of a good Teacher and a good deed. Jesus answered both: only God is good. The Gospels record different parts of one reply.

scene.label: A ruler
scene.text: Luke’s word can describe a synagogue leader or a member of a ruling council; Luke does not say which. Young, rich and respected, the man had everything his world admired.

scene.label: Riches and blessing
scene.text: Many in Israel saw wealth as a sign of God’s favor, remembering Abraham, Job and the blessings promised in Deuteronomy 28. That is why the disciples were so astonished: if a man like this could hardly be saved, who could?

scene.label: The eye of a needle
scene.text: The camel was the largest animal in Palestine and a needle’s eye the smallest opening anyone knew. Jesus describes something impossible, as His next words make clear. The idea of a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle’s Eye has no support in ancient sources.

scene.label: Twelve thrones
scene.text: “The regeneration” means the renewal of all things at the end of the age (compare Acts 3:21). Like the twelve sons of Jacob at the head of Israel, the Twelve would stand at the head of God’s renewed people.

witnesses.matthew: Calls him a young man and records his questions, “Which ones?” and “What do I still lack?” Matthew alone gives the promise of twelve thrones, and he follows at once with the workers in the vineyard, which unfolds the saying about the first and the last.
witnesses.mark: Gives the eyewitness touches: the man running and kneeling, Jesus looking at him and loving him, Jesus looking around at the disciples. Only Mark adds “take up the cross” and the honest note that the hundredfold comes “with persecutions.”
witnesses.luke: Calls him a ruler and says he was “very rich.” A few verses later Luke tells of another rich man in Jericho, Zacchaeus, who gives half his goods away without being asked (19:8).

seeing.reveals: Jesus loves the man who walks away and still does not lower the cost. He claims a place only God can hold: giving everything to the poor is not enough without “come, follow Me.”
seeing.living: This man’s wealth held his heart, and Jesus put His finger on it. He may not ask every disciple to sell everything, but He asks each one to let go of whatever holds the place that belongs to Him. And what is impossible for us, letting go and entering, God can do.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus looked at you with love and said, “One thing you lack,” what would He name?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus lovingly names what holds us, and what is impossible for us, God can do.
outline: A seeker who went away sad (17–22)
A hundredfold for those who leave all (28–31)
preaching.watch_for: Mark notes three looks of Jesus: at the man with love (v. 21), around at the disciples (v. 23), and at them as He answers (v. 27). The passage turns on the word “impossible” in verse 27.

title: The Rich Young Ruler
